content.overview: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 gives a fresh period of limitation where, before the prescribed period expires, the party against whom a property or right is claimed makes a signed written acknowledgement of liability in respect of that property or right. The fresh period is computed from the time the acknowledgement is signed. An acknowledgement may be made before the period expires. A writing after expiry does not start a fresh period under this section. The explanation treats an acknowledgement as signed if it was signed either personally or by an agent duly authorised, and it covers acknowledgements that are undated or that admit a smaller liability.
content.study: Check three things: writing, signature by the party or authorised agent, and a date before expiry. Then compute the fresh period from the signing. Do not treat a part-payment, which is section 19, as an acknowledgement.

learningObjectives: Require a signed writing before expiry.
Compute the fresh period from the signing.
enhancement.definition: Section 18 starts a fresh limitation period from a signed written acknowledgement of liability made before time expires.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The acknowledgement does not revive a period that has already ended. It resets computation only if it is in time, in writing, and signed.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Limitation Act, 1963, section 18. Section 19 is part-payment and is not this topic.
essentialIngredients: Acknowledgement of liability in respect of it
Signed by the party or an agent duly authorised
Made before the prescribed period expires
Fresh period from the time of signing
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 18(1) applies to a suit or application in respect of any property or right. The acknowledgement must be made before expiration of the prescribed period. It must be in writing and signed by the party against whom the property or right is claimed. A fresh period is then computed from the time when the acknowledgement was so signed. The explanation says an acknowledgement may be sufficient though it omits to specify the exact nature of the property or right, or avers that the time for payment has not yet come, or is accompanied by a refusal to pay, or is coupled with a claim to set off, or is addressed to a person other than the person entitled. It also says a signed acknowledgement includes signature by an agent duly authorised, and that an undated acknowledgement may be used if the date can be proved. An oral promise is outside the section. A payment is section 19 if that section's conditions are met.
examples: A debtor signs a ledger acknowledgement in year two of a three-year period. A fresh period runs from that signing.
The same writing is signed after the period has ended. Section 18 does not start a fresh period.
The debtor pays part of the debt without a signed acknowledgement. Look at section 19, not section 18.
enhancement.problemApplication: Find the writing, the signature, and the date. If the date is inside the old period, count afresh from signing. If it is oral or late, section 18 does not apply.
distinctions: Signed writing vs an oral promise
Acknowledgement before expiry vs a writing after expiry

It must be made before expiry.
The fresh period runs from signing.
An agent may sign if duly authorised.
An oral promise is not section 18.
